dossiers.title: Superliminal
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Players characterize the first-person puzzle loop as manipulating object size and position through forced perspective and optical illusions.
The camera-based idea is praised as imaginative but several puzzle-oriented players consider its solutions too easy or insufficiently developed.
Multiple completed-player reports describe a short and largely linear progression through surreal dream rooms, often only several hours long.
Players praise the surreal imagery, dreamlike staging and surprising scenery even when disappointed by the mechanical depth.
Some players feel too many puzzles repeat the same enlarge-shrink tactic and that substantial stretches become a walking experience.
One Russian-language player enjoyed most of the puzzles but singled out a late lift challenge as frustrating.
Russian and English players report contrasting cooperative experiences, including enjoyable shared play but also troublesome maze navigation and multiplayer bugs.
Player expectations divide between an atmospheric, unusual journey and a comparatively demanding Portal-like puzzle game.
Reviewers describe moving through authored stages, with optional commentary available on replay rather than a character build or upgrade system.

dossiers.title: Total War: EMPIRE – Definitive Edition
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Players describe a large historical campaign pairing turn-based territorial, economic and diplomatic strategy with real-time land and naval battles.
Russian and English accounts highlight eighteenth-century musket lines, artillery placement and formation tactics as distinctive battlefield activities.
Campaign advancement focuses on territorial expansion, resource planning, diplomacy, armed forces and managing linked geopolitical theatres.
Some long-term players admire the historical setting and scale so much that they want more minor factions or a modern follow-up.
Players repeatedly identify weak or inconsistent campaign and battle AI, including friendly fire and unreliable troop orders.
Players describe a complicated strategic economy and diplomacy, while veteran battle players also describe scripted or predictable opponents.
Accounts of siege fighting mention poor opponent positioning and troublesome unit pathing in or around fortifications.
Several players value the atmospheric battlefield presentation while still recognizing janky controls and persistent legacy limitations.
The sampled player discussion concentrates on the extensive single-player grand campaign rather than multiplayer as the required primary experience.

dossiers.title: A Monster's Expedition
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 11 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Player descriptions center on cutting trees then pushing or rolling logs to form bridges between separate small islands.
The nonlinear interconnected archipelago lets players branch off to other challenges, postponing obstacles and returning later.
Main-route completion is distinct from more difficult optional museum, island and snowman-related secrets, which may add extensive playtime.
An approachable main path coexists with intricate optional spatial challenges and multi-island log interactions.
Several players praised the gentle atmosphere, quiet soundtrack, colorful islands and humorous museum descriptions of human artifacts.
Players also report that rolling logs through similar small locations for hours can become repetitive even if the premise is charming.
Some reviewers criticize navigation when a neighboring island is apparently reachable but actually requires a different route or later insight.
Positive player reports highlight undo and restart aids, while completionists describe occasional extensive experimentation and using hints.
Accounts distinguish roughly eight-to-twenty-hour main progression from considerably longer attempts to reach every secret island.
Players disagree over museum humor: some enjoy odd interpretations of everyday human artifacts, others dismiss the jokes.
One Russian-language player particularly missed narrative happenings, dialogue and more activity types beyond crossing island after island.
